News.title: Female rapper Tokischa slammed for posing naked in CHURCH for very provocative photoshoot – but she doubles down
News.content:
ALTAR EGO Female rapper Tokischa slammed for posing naked in CHURCH for very provocative photoshoot – but she doubles down

RAPPER Tokischa has sparked fury after stripping off for a provocative photo shoot at a church.

Church bosses blasted the 30-year-old – full name Tokischa Altagracia Peralta – after she was snapped wearing next to nothing inside a basilica.





One outrageous picture shows the rapper kneeling on a pew in nothing more than a skimpy G-string and high heels, flashing her tattoos in front of an image of the Divine Mercy.

Another shows her surrounded by arrows with her back to the wall, possibly referencing the martyrdom of St Sebastian.

The provocative pics were taken during a music video shoot inside the Basilica of Santa María del Coro in San Sebastián, Spain.

The Diocese of San Sebastián has now demanded that the production company remove the racy snaps and is even considering a lawsuit.

A spokesperson said: “We deeply regret the misuse of a sacred space to create content that is at odds with the respect owed to such a place and that offends the religious sensibilities of the faithful.”

Tokischa was filming for her music video (No) Margine – Part 1 – ‘Bisous Bisous’, which premiered to her more than two million subscribers on March 25.

The Diocese claims that last July, production company Visore lied about the nature of the filming.



It claims Visore had requested permission to film a “brief scene inside one of the diocese’s churches, promising it would be a ‘contemplative and respectful moment, with no dialogue or any activity that would disrupt the normal running of the space’.”

When pressed for further details, the company said it was a “cultural project aimed at promoting Basque culture through an intimate, poetic story”.

After checking out Tokischa and Visore’s previous work, the Diocese reportedly refused the request.

But Visore allegedly went behind its back, approaching other officials connected with the basilica without disclosing the refusal.

The Diocese said: “It is being examined whether these actions might require some form of legal or canonical action.



“Only activities that support and promote worship, piety, and religion are permitted in a sacred place, and anything inconsistent with the holiness of the site is prohibited.”

Tokischa, from Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, is no stranger to controversy and has been caught up in similar incidents in the past.

The rapper was slammed in 2021 after she shared pics of her posing semi-naked at the sanctuary of the Virgin of Altagracia in La Vega in her home country.



After the latest backlash, she told fans on social media: “My relationship is with God, not with religion.

“God accepts me as I am, created me, does not judge me, and allows me to learn from my mistakes and discover the truth for myself.”

Tokischa has endured a difficult past, being groomed into sex work as an 18-year-old.

Commenting on the traumatic experience, she told Listin Diario: “Being with a person you aren’t attracted to and like is frustrating.

“After I had sex with someone, I would go into the bathroom to take a shower, crying, frustrated.”



At the time, Tokischa said she would spend the money on drugs, but turned her life around when she began working on music.

She shot to fame after topping the Dominican charts with the single Bellaca Putona in January 2021.

Her international breakthrough came after collaborations with Latin stars J Balvin and Rosalia that summer.

News.title: OAP tourist, 84, killed in horror Canary Islands robbery after arranging meet-up with stranger on app
News.content:
MUGGING HORROR OAP tourist, 84, killed in horror Canary Islands robbery after arranging meet-up with stranger on app

A PENSIONER on holiday was allegedly lured to his death after arranging a meeting on a dating app.

The 84-year-old tourist was robbed and fatally injured during a violent struggle inside his Gran Canaria apartment in Maspalomas.





The elderly visitor had arrived on the island for a vacation when he decided one night in March to install the dating app and arrange a meeting.

But the man he contacted allegedly had a far darker plan.

The meeting turned fatal when the pensioner confronted the man, who supposedly attempted to steal his valuables

During the struggle, the suspect is accused of pushing the elderly tourist, who lost his balance, fell to the ground, and hit his head.

He died from the impact, according to information obtained by LA PROVINCIA/Diario de Las Palmas.

The alleged assailant fled the scene immediately after the fatal incident and went on the run.

He travelled to Tenerife, believing he would be safe.

But officers from the National Police Homicide Unit were already closing in after the body was discovered in Maspalomas.



Spain’s National Police have now arrested the suspected killer in Tenerife.

Investigators say he had downloaded the dating apps again while on the island and may have been planning to target more victims.

Detectives quickly uncovered the exchange of messages between the victim and the suspect, leading them to conclude he was a frequent user of social media and that this may not have been his first offence.

Officers discovered that the suspect had allegedly turned dating apps into a calculated way of targeting victims.

He would charm men online, arrange to meet them in person, and then rob them.



Investigators say he specifically targeted tourists because they were more likely to leave the islands without reporting the crimes.

In one case, he is believed to have stolen £17,400(€20,000) from a victim.

The investigation – which focused heavily on tracking activity across these types of apps – eventually led officers to Tenerife, where the suspect had been hiding.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police managed to apprehend him before he could allegedly meet another potential victim.

The suspect is now in the custody of Spain’s National Police, who say the investigation is continuing until the case is fully resolved.

News.title: Three Russian submarines tracked by Britain off UK shores in North Atlantic for a MONTH before Putin’s sailors retreated
News.content:
VLAD’S TRIPLE THREAT Three Russian submarines tracked by Britain off UK shores in North Atlantic for a MONTH before Putin’s sailors retreated

THREE Russian submarines were tracked by Britain for a whole month before the Navy helped scare away Vladimir Putin’s meddling sailors.

Allied intelligence monitored a Russian attack submarine and two spy submarines nearing undersea cables and pipelines in the North Atlantic, UK Defence Secretary John Healey announced.



Healey proudly praised the UK and its allies in Norway after the successful mission.



The operation involved a frigate, planes and hundreds of personnel who all helped to monitor and deter any threat from the trio of vessels.

Healey sent a clear message to Vladimir Putin during a press conference today as he warned the tyrant: “We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines.

“You should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences.”

Each of the three submarines were tracked “24/7” by at least one Royal Navy warship and Royal Air Force P8 aircraft alongside allies.



“Our armed forces left them in no doubt that they were being monitored, that their movements were not covert,” Healey added.

Putin’s Akula submarine was first to retreat back towards the Kremlin before the two of Moscow’s Main Directorate for Deep Sea Research submarines followed soon after.

News.title: Female support worker, 28, shared bed with schoolboy, filmed them kissing and sent sexual pictures wearing just a towel
News.content:
VILE ABUSE Female support worker, 28, shared bed with schoolboy, filmed them kissing and sent sexual pictures wearing just a towel

A FEMALE support worker shared a bed with a schoolboy and sent him sexual photos of her wearing just a towel.

Chloe Short, 28, was employed to help the 15-year-old’s family when she filmed herself sharing a “sexual” kiss with the teen.





She had been paid to stay overnight at the family address to give the boy’s family some respite.

But a fitness to practice panel was told she behaved in a “in a wholly inappropriate manner”.

One picture Short sent the underage boy showed her in a towel after getting out of the shower.

Another image showed the pair laying in bed together while the boy’s top was off as they shared a “short sexualised kiss”.

Short later messaged him, saying: “Thank you for the cuddles. Had a lush sleep with you.”

She also told him she “missed him every second” and was “obsessed with him”.

The hearing was told Short was working for an organisation that provided support for families and children.

She was assigned to support the vulnerable 15-year-old boy and carried out a series of home visits as a result of her role.



Short’s crimes were exposed when her girlfriend became suspicious about her behaviour and looked through her phone.

She was previously handed a ten month suspended prison sentence after admitting sexual activity with a child.

During her sentencing hearing, a judge told Short her behaviour had been “very inappropriate” and that she had rejected the trust which had been placed in her by virtue of her job.

The support worker, of Caerphilly, Wales, has now been struck off the professional care worker register following a professional standards hearing.

Committee chair Steve Jones said the case was too serious to warrant any sanction other than striking off.



He added: “The offence is so serious there will always be the risk with Miss Short working with vulnerable people.”

News.title: Big mystery creature with hooves washes up on beach after Storm Dave as locals and dog walkers told to stay away
News.content:
SEA RIDDLE Big mystery creature with hooves washes up on beach after Storm Dave as locals and dog walkers told to stay away

THE DECOMPOSING remains of a mysterious carcass were discovered on a beach after Storm Dave ravaged the coastline.

Dog walkers and beach strollers in Anglesey have been told to steer clear of the carcass, which has stumped locals and left many guessing what it belongs to.





While marine mammals make up the majority of carcasses found on coastlines, photographs of the Anglesey specimen show a four-legged skeleton still partially covered in fur.

The photographs were shared online, with one woman remarking that it “didn’t look aquatic”.

Some have suggested the mangled remains belong to either a cow, horse, llama or alpaca.

A gruelling closer inspection revealed a cloven hoof with two distinct toes however, ruling out horse, which has single hooves.

Given its size, the carcass more likely belongs to a deer, a possible escapee from the Bodorgan Estate, the island’s largest estate, some have suggested.

One walker said they would be actively avoiding the grisly sight: “Was planning a walk along the beach from Malltraeth to Abermenai Point – I think I’ll go elsewhere, don’t fancy getting a whiff of that!”

The stunning stretch of coastline belongs to the Newborough National Nature Reserve in the southwest corner of the island.



Anglesey’s recent mystery carcass is not the only find of its kind in Wales.

The ghostly remains of what appeared to be a huge whale carcass stunned visitors when it washed up on a popular beach in Pembrey in September.

Further afield in Scotland the skeleton of a monstrous snake-like creature washed up on a beach at the start of last year, a truly ghoulish sight for passers-by.

Experts ruled out the possibility of it being a marine creature, with one suggesting it belonged to a reticulated python, the longest snake species in the world.

How the non-native species ended up on a beach in Scotland is a mystery.

News.title: How Trump could PUNISH Nato after alliance chief sides with US and says allies were tested and failed over Iran
News.content:
DONALD Trump is reportedly weighing up punishing “unhelpful” Nato nations after he blasted the alliance for “failing” over their response to the Iran war.

Nato chief Mark Rutte said he understands Washington‘s frustrations as he even agreed with Trump, saying: “Not all European nations lived up to those commitments”.





Trump is now said to be mulling over a plan to pull troops out of certain Nato countries and move them to more “supportive” allies, according to the Wall Street Journal.

It comes as

The proposal – which is reportedly still in “early conception” – would fall short of Trump’s recent threats to completely withdraw from the alliance.

By law, the Trump administration wouldn’t be able to remove the US from Nato without Congressional approval first.

It remains unclear what nations could be on Trump’s chopping block but he has shared fiery exchanges with leaders such as Britain’s Keir Starmer and Spain’s Pedro Sanchez in recent weeks.

The startling claims came as Rutte held top-secret talks with Trump on Wednesday as they reportedly spoke in the White House about the future of Nato.

Rutte, known in Europe as the “Trump whisperer”, was seen entering the West Wing through a side gate before the doors were tightly shut behind him.



The talks came after White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt quoted Trump as saying yesterday: “Nato was tested and they failed.”

She added that it was “sad that Nato has turned their backs on the American people”.

Rutte was asked if he agreed that allies had failed the US to which he replied: “Some of them ‌yes, ⁠but a large majority of European countries, and that’s what we discussed today, have done what ​they promised ​before ⁠in a case like this.”

The secretary general has tried to calm down concerns of an unfixable rift among members with his trip to Washington the latest attempt.

He revealed he had a “frank and open” discussion with Trump as he told CNN: “Not all European nations lived up to those commitments and I completely understand he is disappointed about it.”



He added: “I was also able to point to the fact that the large majority of European nations has been helpful with basing, with logistics, with overflights, with making sure that they live up to the commitments.”

A short time after the meeting, Trump issued a furious statement over Nato.



He said: “Nato wasn’t there when we needed them and they won’t be there if we need them again.”

Trump then directly mentioned Greenland in the Truth Social post after months of the US publicly trying to seize the island from Denmark.

The US president has previously vowed to take the Danish overseas territory “the hard way” if the Danes didn’t hand over control.

Denmark – a proud Nato member – called on its allies to condemn Trump’s comments as they warned if the US did start an invasion then it would invoke Article 5.

Article 5 is an agreed deal between all the allies stating that an armed attack against a member would be considered an attack against all.



The Iran war has piled even more pressure on the alliance with Trump left berating some members over their slow response to his conflict.

He has spent weeks asking for Nato warships to be sent to the Strait of Hormuz to help reopen the vital trade waterway after Iran blocked it off.

The US also called on allies – such as the UK and France – to support the conflict and allow the American military to use air bases closer to the Gulf.

Trump said last week he was on the verge of leaving Nato after the alliance’s “terrible” show of support in the Middle East.



Experts warned The Sun last week that pulling the US out of Nato would be among the “worst crises in the alliance’s history” and spark months of panic.

Rutte also had to step in back in January after Trump launched a dig at his European allies claiming they “stayed off the front lines” in Afghanistan.

Trump’s current secretary of state, Marco Rubio also met separately with Rutte on Wednesday morning for their own top-secret meeting at the State Department.

In a statement, the State Department said Rubio and Rutte had discussed the war with Iran, along with US efforts to negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and increasing coordination and burden shifting with Nato allies.



One of the main areas of concern between Nato and the US across in Iran is over the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump blasted Nato allies as “cowards” as he called the group “terrible”, telling fuel-starved members to “get your own oil” from the Strait of Hormuz.

British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who has been a particular source of Trump’s frustration, is in the Gulf now to discuss the war with allies.

He told Gulf allies Iran must not “hold the Strait of Hormuz to ransom” in a regional defence call during his visit.

As Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper demanded the Strait of Hormuz has no tolls placed on it by Iran after it was reported the regime was instating a “toll booth” system for passing vessels.



What has sparked the US-Nato rift? DONALD Trump has gone on several furious tirades against Nato ever since launching Operation Epic Fury at the end of February on Iran. Most of these verbal attacks feature the US president accusing his allies of not supporting him during the war. He has been vocal about wanting help from Nato warships – especially the UK – to reopen the Strait of Hormuz which Tehran has blocked off. Trump blasted Nato allies as “cowards” after they refused to send ships to the Middle East. He said on Truth Social: “NATO NATIONS HAVE DONE ABSOLUTELY NOTHING TO HELP WITH THE LUNATIC NATION, NOW MILITARILY DECIMATED, OF IRAN.” The war has also caused Trump to engage with Nato leaders such as Britain’s Keir Starmer and Spain’s Pedro Sanchez. Trump called Sir Keir “no Winston Churchill” as he slammed the UK PM for his reluctance over letting the US use Brit bases to attack Tehran. He then threatened to halt all trade with Spain after PM Sanchez declared he would bar the US from using its military bases as part of operations in Iran. “We don’t want anything to do with Spain,” he added. Even before the war in Iran kicked off, Trump hit out at Nato as he claimed some allies “stayed off the front lines” in Afghanistan. The alliance responded by reminding him that hundreds of allied troops were killed fighting shoulder-to-shoulder with US forces. The war in Ukraine has also been a major point of difference within Nato. Trump claimed last September Nato has never been 100 per cent committed to ending the conflict – as he tried his best to hash out a peace deal. He ordered the alliance to apply the pressure on Putin as he even promised: “If Nato does as I say, the WAR will end quickly, and all of those lives will be saved!”

Cooper told the BBC: “One of the crucial things that the prime minister will be talking to Gulf partners about is the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz which is crucial for our Gulf partners.

“It is their trading route but it’s also vital for the global economy and no country should be able to hijack those international shipping transit routes in the way that Iran has.

“That’s why it’s so important we have this international cooperation to keep up the pressure to get the strait fully open.

“Not to have tolls, not to have restrictions, but to get that fully reopened.”

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz remains a top priority for all nations who rely on the global trade route for goods such as oil.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Iran had unblocked the waterway for a few hours before they closed it again after Israel blitzed their allies in Lebanon.

The regime has now released a chilling map showing how tankers will be forced to weave through deadly sea mines dotted throughout the Strait.

News.title: Paedo ex-BBC presenter who carried out sick sex attacks on children jailed again for meeting up with teen
News.content:
BEHIND BARS Paedo ex-BBC presenter who carried out sick sex attacks on children jailed again for meeting up with teen

A PAEDO ex-BBC presenter who carried out a string of sick sex attacks on children has been jailed again for meeting up with a teen.

Peter Rowell, 67, was jailed for six years in 2012 for 12 charges of indecent assault on girls under the age of 16.





He also admitted six counts of making an indecent photograph of a child after he was found with over 400 twisted images.

Rowell, who presented the Afternoon Show on BBC Radio Bristol, was ordered to sign the sex offender register.

But he has now been locked up for 29 weeks after he pleaded guilty to two counts of breaching sex offender notification requirements.

The court heard he breached the order by being at a property for over 12 hours with a child under 18 with or without an adult.

Rowell also travelled 30 miles from his home in Abergavenny, Monmouthshire, to stay at an address without telling police his whereabouts.

The breaches come over a decade after he was jailed for the sickening child sex crimes.

Rowell targeted the underage girls between 1989 and the early 1990s and abused his position as a “minor celebrity“.

He invited his victims to visit his studio after they contacted him to find out more about his work in the media.



Rowell, who was also a news bulletin reader on ITV West for more than 10 years and worked as a DJ for commercial radio station GWR in the 1980s, would then sexually abuse the youngsters.

The broadcaster sparked a nationwide search after failing to turn up for work in March 2011.

His car was discovered left in a supermarket car park before Rowell was later found in Keswick, Cumbria, and arrested.

Before his disappearance, police had raided his home and seized his computer where they found hundreds of indecent images of children.

Sentencing him in 2012, Judge David Ticehurst said: “You had a life and lifestyle that would have been the envy of many – an apparently successful career in a glamorous and glittering world.



“Behind that public image you were a man that hid a dark secret. You were attracted to young girls, sexually abusing and exploiting for your own gratification.

“You were someone prepared to use the world of showbiz to attract young girls to you to abuse them.

“It is not a case of you involving yourself with a star-struck teenager on an isolated occasion and succumbing to temptation but a series of offences involving five separate girls over a period of five years.”

News.title: Heartwarming pics show amazing recovery of 250 poodles left to die in squalid home
News.content:
NEW heartwarming pictures show the incredible recovery of 250 poodle-cross dogs after they were found living in their own filth in a dingy home.

The conditions were so shocking that the RSPCA was forced to deny the image of the “severely matted” dogs was AI-generated.





An “extremely vulnerable, elderly owner” had kept the large number of poodles in cramped conditions, with many of them covered in their own filth and suffering from sore skin and matted coats.

But thankfully some kind-hearted dog lovers have adopted some of the poodles, giving them a brand new life.

Their new owners shared adorable pictures of the canines heartwarming transformations.



One sweet mutt, now called Ravi, is shown lounging on an armchair – clearly enjoying his new life.

Another poodle named Lily is seen relaxing on the sofa next to her new owner and canine-friend.

Meanwhile, a cute image of a rescue shows the sweet dog sitting on a grey blanket next to its new toy and tennis ball.

Rex, another dog that was adopted, has “grown in body and confidence” according to his new owner.



They continued: “Ours is doing so well, the RSPCA did an amazing job helping him and now us as he navigates his new normal.”

Thankfully, Radcliffe Animal Centre in Nottinghamshire said many of the dogs have now been reserved or taken to new homes.

But sadly two poodles – Eva and Teddy – are still at the rescue home waiting to find new owners.

Others found living in the disgusting conditions were sent to other RSPCA centres including Stevie – a deaf and blind cocker spaniel – and Sandy, a poodle.

Stevie relies on his best pal Sandy, who has become her guide, to navigate the world.



The pair received a visit from reality TV star Kate Lawler, who said: “Stevie is such a brave and beautiful dog and I really hope she and Sandy find the perfect home together.

“It’s just amazing the way Sandy helps look after Stevie.



“I was so taken with their story, and the unbelievable situation they were rescued from.

“It’s a reminder of the dangers of multi-animal households when things aren’t kept under control, but I am so relieved that so many of the animals will get a second chance of forever home happiness.

When the RSPCA first shared the images of the dogs, viewers were shocked at the state home they were being kept in.

The defenceless animals were stuffed into every nook of the decrepit home, which is covered in fur with wallpaper peeling from the walls.

When they were rescued, some were so terrified of the outside world that they had to be carried from their kennels to the grass.



The huge pack belonged to a single family who lost control of their breeding, sparking a shocking spiral in numbers.

Officials say the situation quickly got out of hand due to extenuating family circumstances, with living conditions deteriorating as the number of dogs soared.



The rescue took place at an undisclosed location.

RSPCA Superintendent Jo Hirst said: “Over-breeding and overwhelmed owners can create staggering situations, and our officers are seeing more cases involving 10, 20, even 100 animals.”

The charity said over-breeding had taken over, causing living conditions to “spiral out of control”.

It said they responded to 75 separate incidents involving 100 animals or more last year.

These “extremely large-scale rescues” have left the charity with a “capacity crisis” and they are urging more owners to adopt.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The RSPCA added: “There can be many reasons why people end up with far more animals than they can care for, such as mental health conditions, disability, bereavements, and serious financial issues.

“These cases are often complex, and the people involved need help and support to get back onto the right path or to access the services they need themselves.”

News.title: Doctor Amir Khan issues advice to anyone who needs the loo 'all the time'
News.content:
Doctor Amir Khan issues advice to anyone who needs the loo 'all the time'

An estimated five million people in England alone suffer from it - but help is at hand

View Image The NHS describes urinary frequency as the 'need to pass urine often and more frequently than usual and in small volumes'

A doctor has offered fresh hope for those who find themselves needing the toilet constantly. According to the Urology Foundation, an estimated 5 million people in England are affected by overactive bladder (OAB).

‌



OAB is a 'common condition characterised by urgent and frequent urination'. It can also include urge incontinence where there is involuntary leakage following an urgent need to urinate.

‌



While it may appear trivial, the condition can profoundly affect people's day-to-day lives. However, Dr Amir Khan, an NHS GP well known for his social media guidance and daytime TV appearances, insists there are steps you can take to tackle the problem.

‌



"If you're someone who does a just-in-case wee, just before leaving the house, maybe before a meeting, or before bed, sometimes even twice, this is really important for you," he said. "It might actually be making your bladder symptoms worse. I see this all the time in clinic. People going again even when they've just been because it feels safer than risking urgency or waking up in the middle of the night to go.

"But here's what's really happening: your bladder is a muscle and it works with your nerves to tell your brain when it's full. Now normally, that signal up to your brain shouldn't come until your bladder is holding around 300 to 500 millilitres of urine. But, if you keep emptying it early-you know, those just-in-case wees - you start to retrain that system between your bladder and your brain. And over time, your bladder gets used to being emptied at lower volumes.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"I always say to my patients: it's like a car alarm that's become too sensitive. At first, it only goes off when there's a real threat, but then it starts going off at everything: a gust of wind, someone just walking past. That's what your bladder is doing. It starts sending "I need to go now" signals even when it's barely full.", reports Lancs Live.

"That's how urgency and urge incontinence develop or get worse. Because instead of emptying everything, you're teaching your bladder to signal to your brain you need to go earlier and earlier. So you end up waking up in the middle of the night needing to go even when your bladder isn't that full and even though you went before you went to bed - you might not have needed to, but you went anyway."

So what does the NHS have to say on the matter?

The NHS says: "An overactive bladder is where a person regularly gets a sudden and compelling need or desire to pass urine. This sensation is difficult to put off (defer) and this can happen at any time during the day or night, often without any warning.

‌



"If you have urinary frequency, this means that you need to pass urine often and more frequently than usual and in small volumes. The number of times people normally have to pass urine each day varies but most people pass urine 6-8 times per day. However, 4-10 times per day can also be normal if you are happy and healthy with the number of times you visit the toilet.

"Normal urine frequency depends on how much you drink in the day and what types of fluid you drink. You may all pass urine more frequently if you are taking certain medications such as diuretics. People with overactive bladders tend to pass urine more often than they would expect during the daytime.

"Overactive bladder can also cause you to get up more than twice per night to pass urine. During your sleep time you should have 6-8 hours of uninterrupted sleep. Sometimes disturbed nights can be the main problem. Urinary tract problems other than OAB can also cause nocturia, so this symptom may persist even if other OAB problems respond to treatment.

‌



"OAB is common and can affect people of all ages, including children and the elderly. Around 12% of the total adult population suffer with OAB. Usually, the cause is unknown. Anxiety can make the problem worse. The types of fluid that you drink can also influence your symptoms. People with neurological disease are at a particularly higher risk of OAB."

What can be done about it?

Dr Khan explains: "So what's the solution? Well, you need to retrain the alarm system. That's bladder training. Try to cut down on those just-in-case wees. Stick to going every three or four hours rather than constantly, and space out those wees more and more. If urgency hits: pause, breathe, stay still, let it pass before going to the toilet. You're teaching your bladder this isn't an emergency.

"And also, don't forget: reduce caffeine, avoid large drinks right before bed, and those pelvic floor exercises. This all takes time. Most people notice a small improvement in two to four weeks, but it can take six to twelve weeks to really retrain that bladder.

Article continues below

"And this is how I describe pelvic floor exercises to my patients - bear with me," he added. "Right, you're on the toilet having a wee, you're halfway through, and then the doorbell goes and it's an Amazon driver or a delivery that you've been waiting ages for; you can't miss it, so you have to hold in your wee halfway through and run downstairs. Those are your front pelvic floor muscles.

"Now, you're holding them in, and you're in a lift now and Rihanna walks in and you need to fart, but you can't fart in front of Rihanna, so you're holding in a fart and you're holding in that halfway wee too. Those are your back and front pelvic floor exercises. Train them well." According to the NHS, should you visit a doctor regarding this issue, they will discuss both your specific problem and your overall health. They may also carry out a physical examination and test your urine for any signs of infection.

You will additionally be required to keep a three-day bladder diary, logging when you urinate and the volume passed. A flow test and post void ultrasound may also be recommended. For this, you'll be asked to urinate into a specialist machine that monitors both the strength and volume of your flow. A post void ultrasound will then measure the quantity of urine remaining in your bladder (if any) following urination.

News.title: 'I was diagnosed with cancer linked to sex I'd had decades earlier'
News.content:
'I was diagnosed with cancer linked to sex I'd had decades earlier'

Jeff Bradford, 62, thought dust from gym renovations caused his persistent sore throat in 2016 but doctors discovered it was stage-three throat cancer likely linked to sex he'd had years before

View 4 Images Jeff Bradford was diagnosed with throat cancer several years ago (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

A father who initially put a persistent sore throat down to dust from refurbishing his gym was stunned to discover it was actually throat cancer – linked by the HPV16 virus contracted through oral sex.

‌



Jeff Bradford, 62, first experienced a tickly throat after working on the rafters of his gym in March 2016. He explained: "We were in the loft putting some equipment up onto the rafters and there was a lot of dust and insulation. I had a mask but a couple of days after I had a bit of a sore throat and I thought it was just the dust but I couldn't shake it." He initially attempted gargling soluble aspirin, believing it was an ordinary sore throat.

‌



After a fortnight without improvement, Jeff consulted his GP, who diagnosed "classic tonsillitis" and prescribed antibiotics. When the symptoms continued, he returned to see a different doctor, who provided a stronger dose and took a throat swab, ultimately referring him to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

‌



"They must have seen the photos and thought 'there's something dodgy going on there'. I couldn't see anything but I could feel something touching the back of my tongue, it was making me gag. It was like something was tickling the back of my tongue."

View 4 Images Jeff initially blamed his sore throat on dust (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

At the hospital, a specialist examined Jeff and scheduled him for a biopsy. While on the operating table, the surgeon informed him the thumb-sized mass at the back of his throat had doubled in size since the previous scan and recommended immediate removal. "The surgeon came up that evening [after the surgery] and he said 'looking at it, I think you've got stage three cancer' I was just shocked," Jeff said.

‌



After the four-hour operation, tests confirmed stage-three throat cancer. Doctors told Jeff the cancer had been triggered by the HPV16 strain, which can be passed on through sexual activity, most commonly oral sex.

"A week later I went back and that's when they mentioned HPV, I didn't know what that was. HPV is caught through sexual transmission, it's normally from oral sex. I was totally shocked it was from that," Jeff said, adding that doctors believed he had contracted the virus decades before, prior to meeting his wife Heidi Bradford.

View 4 Images Jeff with wife Heidi

‌



Jeff endured chemotherapy and 35 rounds of radiotherapy, leaving him bed-bound for three months. He continued: "Radiotherapy caused really bad burns. It was like someone took a blowtorch to my neck, it was horrible. I went home and went to bed for three months".

Now a decade clear of cancer, Jeff is urging others not to brush aside persistent symptoms, saying: "If someone has a persistent sore throat my advice is to get it checked out, it could be easily missed if you don't push it. Everybody does it, don't they?

"It's a normal, sexual activity with somebody you love... I would never say to anyone 'give up oral sex'... but it might put people off that. I think if it's not talked about quite candidly it'll get brushed under the carpet and if people are embarrassed to talk about it they may avoid treatment."

‌



View 4 Images Jeff's neck after undergoing radiotherapy (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

Jeff, a former Royal Air Force corporal and father-of-two from Forres, Moray, Scotland, put his diagnosis down to simply "bad luck".

He continued: "I've had a few partners before I met my wife, but you just go about life like everyone else. You don't expect when you're young 'do that and I might get cancer when I'm 50-odd'."

Article continues below

What is HPV?

According to the NHS, human papillomavirus (HPV) is a collection of viruses that affect the skin and moist membranes, including the cervix, anus, mouth, and throat. It is most commonly transmitted through sexual activity, including oral sex, and can trigger cellular changes that may develop into cancers, such as cervical or potentially throat cancer.

News.title: Answering 'nasty' voice 'cloning' phone call could rob you of all your money
News.content:
Answering 'nasty' voice 'cloning' phone call could rob you of all your money

People should be on high alert and avoid this situation at all costs

View 2 Images Anyone with a mobile phone could become a victim (Image: Getty)

Which? experts claim that people who answer a seemingly innocent phone call could see their bank accounts "drained" as part of a "nasty" scam. The person on the other end of the line may claim to be conducting a lifestyle survey, but they do not care about any of your answers and are only interested in two things.

‌



At some point during the call, people are asked to hand over their bank account details, including the account number and sort code. But that is only half of the scam, as victims also have their identity secretly 'cloned'.

‌



A Which? spokesperson explained: "While you answer the questions, this information is used to create a sophisticated AI-generated clone of your voice. This information is then passed on or sold to another criminal group along with your voice clone."

‌



With all these details, and a lifelike copy of your voice, scammers pose as a legitimate-looking company and set up a direct debit in your name. They use the voice 'clone' created from the survey responses to bypass bank security systems and slowly siphon off cash without some people ever realising.

The spokesperson for Which? said: "Nothing is flagged by your bank because the details are correct. Now your hard-earned cash is going directly into the hands of the fraudsters."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



How can I protect myself and others from this?

The easiest way to avoid getting caught up in this is not to respond to any calls you were not expecting - especially ones from numbers you do not recognise. Answering just one unsolicited spam call will likely lead to more, as it signals to these cold callers that you are an active and valid phone number, marking you as a "live" lead to be targeted again or sold to other scammers.

Which? suggests that people may be able to speak with their phone provider about call-blocking options. They said: "Androids have a setting called 'Filter Spam Calls' and iPhone's have 'Silence unknown callers'."

View 2 Images Hang up if you are worried that a call might lead to a scam (Image: Getty)

Article continues below

If someone answers the phone to someone who claims to be from their bank, the best advice is to hang up right away - especially if it is a call you were not expecting. Which? said that people can call 159 and ask to speak with their genuine banking provider.

The scheme guides people through a list of options to select from to transfer to the verified customer service department. And, to prevent scams going unnoticed and claiming more victims, report the incident to reportfraud.police.uk or call 0300 123 2040.

Even if the scam was unsuccessful, and you were not conned out of any money, it is still worth reporting. This could help raise awareness for others who may have, or become, victims.

News.title: New 'free' change coming to all UK Holland and Barrett stores in '15 mins' update
News.content:
New 'free' change coming to all UK Holland and Barrett stores in '15 mins' update

Customers will be able to take advantage of the 'free' Wellness Check-Ins every month

View 3 Images Every Holland and Barrett store will now offer free Wellness Check-ins (Image: Getty )

A major change is coming to every Holland and Barrett store across the country. It comes as a new national health study found that while 74% of people agree that establishing good health habits now is key to preventing illness in the future, only 50% proactively manage their health.

‌



To help Brits take control of their health, the retailer is launching 300,000 free in-store Wellness Check-Ins per month, available nationwide, as part of its Back Your Body campaign. The store says the new check-ins mark an initiative to move the UK from 'reactive repair to proactive health', and appointments can be made in-store or booked online and last 15 minutes.

‌



A Holland and Barrett spokesperson said the free Wellness Check-Ins will provide science-backed, personalised advice to help people better understand their bodies. The appointments are also designed to "cut through complex information (and wellness misinformation), and turn it into simple, actionable steps".

‌



The Wellness Check-Ins are aimed at helping under-40s, who are not eligible for the NHS 40+ Health Check, "to take control of their health earlier". Up to 4,500 trained 'Wellness Champions' have been enrolled for appointments with customers.

While the in-store Wellness Check-Ins have only just been launched, Holland and Barrett already offers free online appointments for customers. It website explains: "Our advisors are trained and certified to provide advice and are able to make personalised product recommendation. Our training has been verified by external and internal scientific experts and medical practitioners.

View 3 Images Holland and Barrett aims to back the nation’s bodies with a new multi-million pound health commitment to help the public

‌



A spokesperson added that a new national health report suggests that access to healthcare - and therefore preventative health - is increasingly becoming a 'postcode lottery'. The stats are stark and show the pressure on the NHS currently, findings include:

While 56% of Londoners find it easy to access health care, this drops to just 34% in Northern Ireland and 39% in the East Midlands and South East.

83% say they only go to the doctor when absolutely necessary (Wales) vs London (71%).

Health pressure is concentrated in the North East, Yorkshire and Humber, where over one third describe their health as fair or poor.

Dr Carrie Ruxton, award-winning dietician and report contributor, said: "The UK is living longer but not always living well, with a growing burden of preventable disease and health outcomes that lag behind comparable nations. This situation is detrimental for individuals, the workforce, and the NHS.

‌



"Proactive health habits formed in early adulthood can shape long-term health outcomes and positively impact the future burden of chronic disease. However, without accessible, trusted and practical support, many people remain stuck in a cycle of reactive repair."

View 3 Images Checks can cover nutrition, weight, joints, bones, muscles, energy, women’s health and more

Anthony Houghton, Group CEO at Holland and Barrett, said: "We recognise the UK faces a growing health paradox, but Britain isn’t lacking motivation – it’s lacking momentum. The risk is becoming a nation that waits until something goes wrong. To make prevention work, support must be embedded in places people already go, before they become patients – and that infrastructure already exists on the high street.

Article continues below

"This means recognising the role of trusted, community-based support alongside formal healthcare. As the UK’s leading health and wellness retailer, we’re well placed on the high street and online to help the nation back their bodies and make preventative health a reality for all.

"Throughout my career, I’ve learned many lessons along the way, one of the most important being that if I look after my body now, it’ll stay well for longer. I’m a firm believer in prehab over rehab, but the overload of health and wellness information can be overwhelming.

Double World Heptathlon Champion and Olympic silver medalist, Katarina Johnson-Thompson, said: "Holland and Barrett's new Wellness Check-Ins are a great place to start with advice you can trust".

News.title: UK following Russia subs over fears they'll sabotage internet and energy cables
News.content:
UK following Russia subs over fears they'll sabotage internet and energy cables

UK armed forces were deployed to track and deter 'malign activity' by Russian submarines in a massive month-long operation, Defence Secretary John Healey has announced

View 2 Images Defence Secretary John Healey has announced UK armed forces tracked Russian submarines (Image: PA)

UK armed forces were deployed to track and deter "malign activity" by Russian submarines in a massive month-long operation, Defence Secretary John Healey has announced.

‌



UK and allies monitored a Russian attack submarine and two spy submarines in the North Atlantic for a month before they retreated.

‌



Keir Starmer said the UK "will not shy away from taking action" against Russia. And in a direct message to Vladimir Putin, Mr Healey said: "We see you. We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines."

‌



An undersea network of cables and pipelines are vital to the UK, carrying 99% of international telecoms and data traffic, as well as half the gas that heats our homes. This underpins global banking, trade, and communications. There is no evidence any damage has been done to the cables or pipelines.

Iran war live: Ceasefire on brink as Trump lashes out and UK issues urgent warning READ MORE :

View 2 Images Russian vessel Yantar is a specialist reconnaissance ship which carries two unmanned subs (Image: MOD/AFP via Getty Images)

British aircraft and warships identified a Russian attack submarine entering international waters in the High North several weeks ago and tracked its activity around the clock.

‌



Service personnel quickly established that the submarine was deployed as a distraction and the UK worked closely with allies – including Norway – to identify and monitor other Russian undersea naval units conducting "nefarious activity over critical undersea infrastructure elsewhere", the Ministry of Defence said.

Britain's military operation lasted more than a month and has now concluded. More than 5,000 British personnel were involved in the response.

Russia's vessels were from the Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research (known as GUGI), a secretive Russian agency that operates a number of specialised submarines.

‌



British defences were previously tested by GUGI when the Russian spy ship Yantar sailed near UK waters last year. The ship was tracked by a Royal Navy frigate and RAF P8s, with lasers being directed at British pilots.

The Prime Minister said: "I am determined to protect the British people from paying the price for Putin's aggression in their household bills. That is why we will not shy away from taking action and exposing Russia's destabilising activity that seeks to test our resolve.

"Our Armed Forces are among the best in the world, and the British public should be in no doubt that this government will do whatever it takes to defend our national and economic security, wherever in the world that is needed."

Article continues below

The UK is stepping up on its commitment to protect our critical underwater infrastructure. This includes an additional £100 million to support our vital P8 submarine hunting aircraft.

News.title: People are removing 1 plant from gardens in April as it 'implies they're swingers'
News.content:
People are removing 1 plant from gardens in April as it 'implies they're swingers'

People are removing a common plant from their gardens as it's said to imply they could be swingers. Many are stepping into action in April to remedy the supposed issue

View Image People are digging up the common plant (stock image) (Image: Dzurag via Getty Images)

People have begun uprooting a particular plant from their gardens after discovering it carries a rather unlikely connotation. The widespread plant is a familiar sight in gardens throughout the country, yet many are unaware it can lead others to assume they're swingers.

‌



TikTok has recently been flooded with viral videos of people removing the plant from their gardens, with horticultural experts including NGS Gardening demonstrating the correct removal technique. Meanwhile, one Reddit user previously explained their own decision to dig theirs up, leaving many readers rather taken aback.

‌



It appears homeowners are removing the plant for one specific reason, with April considered an ideal time to tackle the task. This isn't the first time the issue has surfaced either, as people previously admitted they didn't know about the plant's hidden meaning.

‌



One social media user wrote: "Bought a house and dug out a massive pampas grass, because we are definitely not swingers! How do I get grass to fill the hole?"

The post sparked considerable debate, with many commenters admitting they were completely unaware of the plant's alleged symbolism.

‌



One user remarked: "Was it hard to remove? We've just bought a house with three huge ones and I hate them." The original poster responded: "I sawed through it with hedge cutters to about two foot tall and then it took me about an hour to dig out from there.

"It was an effort. Just couldn't look it at it any longer!"

Another expressed their bewilderment, simply posting: "Swingers?" Someone clarified: "Having a pampas grass allegedly used to signal to people that you enjoyed swinging. E.g. partner swapping."

‌



A third also remarked: "This is making me cackle." What you might not know is that for decades, having pampas grass in your garden was rumoured to indicate you're a swinger.

It's a well-known British urban myth, believed to originate from 1970s and 1980s suburban culture when these towering plants were supposedly a discreet signal to neighbours with similar interests. While some regard it as an amusing tale, others still prefer not to have it present.

What you should know

Beyond its unconventional alleged associations, homeowners might also be clearing pampas grass now because it's an optimal time for the task. April is regarded as a perfect month to remove or trim back pampas grass, falling within the prime "late winter to early spring" period before fresh, green shoots fully emerge.

‌



Cutting it back now allows you to clear away the dead, weathered and potentially decay-prone foliage from winter. The essential approach is using sharp loppers or an electric hedge trimmer to reduce the plant to roughly six to eight inches (15cm to 20cm) above ground level.

When undertaking this work, always wear robust gardening gloves, long sleeves and eye protection, as pampas grass features razor-sharp leaves that can readily slice skin. Meanwhile, if you're removing it for division purposes, spring is an excellent time to excavate the root ball.

By April, winter conditions have typically rendered the plant simpler to trim back. This is precisely why it's advisable to attempt the task now.

Article continues below

Should you require additional guidance, get in touch with a professional gardener. They can assist you with removal if you find it difficult to manage yourself.

News.title: UK drivers urged to fill up before Thursday 5pm as fuel prices skyrocket
News.content:
UK drivers urged to fill up before Thursday 5pm as fuel prices skyrocket

The average price of diesel has now surpassed 190p a litre, having surged by more than a third since the start of the Iran war, with petrol also continuing to rise

View 2 Images This is the best time to fill up your car amid rising fuel costs (Image: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock)

UK motorists are being advised to fill up their tanks before Thursday evening as fuel prices reach their highest levels in years - despite a significant fall in global oil prices following a US-Iran ceasefire announcement.

The average price of diesel across the UK has topped 190p per litre, having rocketed by more than a third since the start of the Iran war, according to new figures. The average diesel price stood at 191.11p on Thursday morning, up more than 34 per cent since February 28, the RAC revealed.

Petrol was also continuing to climb, with average unleaded prices hitting 158.1p, with an ominous forecast that this is likely to rise again.

View 2 Images Fuel prices are reaching the highest levels since the Iran war (Image: Getty Images)

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said: "Both fuels are now at their most expensive since late 2022. The conditional ceasefire announcement may have taken some heat out of global oil prices, but the outlook for drivers in the UK remains highly uncertain.

"The best hope in the short-term is that pump prices stop rising at the rate they have been and hopefully top out in the coming days."

The spike follows the outbreak of the Iran conflict on February 28, which forced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway responsible for handling approximately 20 per cent of the world's daily oil supply.

The blockade has disrupted the transportation of Middle Eastern oil and gas supplies, sending energy costs sharply upwards. Global oil prices tumbled sharply last week following the announcement by the US and Iran of a conditional two-week ceasefire agreement requiring the strait to be reopened to the US.

Benchmark Brent crude prices fell by roughly 13 per cent to $94.80 (£70.73) per barrel, while US-traded oil plummeted more than 15 per cent to $95.75.

Despite the decline, oil prices remain higher than the levels seen when the conflict first broke out, when costs stood at approximately $70 per barrel. Experts have warned that motorists will need to be patient before feeling the full benefits at the pumps, with many expecting it will be a fortnight before prices drop considerably.

Article continues below

In the meantime, drivers can ease the financial burden by being savvy about when they fill up. William Fletcher, CEO of Car.co.uk, said: "Prices usually rise on Thursday evening and stay elevated through Sunday. If you can plan ahead and fill up mid-week instead, you'll typically save 2-3 pence per litre, which adds up quickly over a year of driving."

The Department for Energy figures are compiled as part of a weekly fuel price survey that has been running since 2003, covering around 60% of the total market volume sold, with average prices calculated every Monday.

News.title: Diabetes risk 'increased by 35pc' for people with common problems
News.content:
Diabetes risk 'increased by 35pc' for people with common problems

A new study has found links

View 3 Images Insomnia was found to be one link (Image: Pexels)

People who are lonely, have trouble sleeping and have mental health problems such as depression and anxiety may face a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes, a study suggests. The link may be down to how the body responds to chronic stress, according to researchers.

‌



Behavioural and psychological factors are “often overlooked” when it comes to predicting disease risk, experts said, but could “provide meaningful signals”. The study, led by researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), analysed lifestyle and health data from 19,774 adults included in the UK Biobank and tracked for up to 17 years.

‌



The team used artificial intelligence (AI) to predict and simulate the development of type 2 diabetes using behaviour, diet and psychological factors. The study found that loneliness, insomnia and poor mental health were estimated to increase diabetes risk by 35 percentage points each.

‌



When all three factors were combined, the estimated risk was 78 percentage points. According to the study, psychological factors “likely reflect” well-established responses to chronic stress, including inflammation, an inability to maintain blood sugar levels and the overproduction of the stress hormone cortisol.

The effects also “underscore” that psychosocial distress is not just a mental challenge, but a “potent metabolic disruptor with real and measurable health consequences”, researchers said. There was also a link between the three psychological stressors and diet.

View 3 Images Depression was a factor (Image: Pexels)

‌



People were more likely to eat more salty, sugary cereals and processed meats when impacted by loneliness, insomnia and mental health issues, which can all lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

Dr Mahreen Kiran, lead author and postgraduate researcher at ARU, said: “This study shows the importance of including behavioural and psychosocial variables such as loneliness, sleep disruption and mental health history within health datasets used for risk prediction. These factors are often overlooked, yet they provide meaningful signals about future disease risk.”

Some 4.6 million people in the UK have a diabetes diagnosis, although estimates suggest a further 1.3 million could be living with undiagnosed type 2 diabetes.

‌



Professor Barbara Pierscionek, deputy dean for research and innovation in the Faculty of Health, Medicine and Social Care at ARU, said: “Type 2 diabetes is a rising global health concern which we know is heavily influenced by lifestyle. However, current risk prediction models rely on BMI, age and blood pressure, which over-simplify this disease and overlook the more complex interconnected behavioural and emotional factors that precede and shape the onset of the condition.”

View 3 Images Anxiety was also found to be connected (Image: Pexels)

The study, published in Frontiers in Digital Health, used a digital twin model, which uses AI to replicate a patient’s health profile and simulate the progression of disease and how effective interventions may be.

Article continues below

Prof Pierscionek added: “Digital twin model systems replicate an individual’s health profiles, enabling us to test ‘what-if’ scenarios and tailor care to individual needs.

"However, most of these existing models rely on real-time data from wearable devices, which can be a barrier for settings lacking in technical infrastructure or underserved communities that struggle with costs.

"Digital twin model systems present a viable cost-effective way of diagnosis, testing and treatment for a number of conditions.”

The UK has issued a stark warning to Vladimir Putin after Russian attack and spy submarines were found operating in the North Atlantic.

Defence secretary John Healey revealed UK and allies monitored the vessels - which included one attack submarine and two spy submarines - for a month before they retreated.

Mr Healey told a press conference in Downing Street on Thursday that in the past few weeks – while many eyes were trained on the Middle East crisis – the UK, in partnership with Norway and other allies, responded to “increased Russian activity” in the Atlantic north of the UK.

Addressing the Russian president directly, Mr Healey said: “We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences.”

open image in gallery Defence Secretary John Healey (Toby Shepheard/PA) ( PA Wire )

It comes after the Telegraph reported that Russia sent a warship to escort sanctioned oil tankers through the English channel, despite Keir Starmer’s warning that sanctioned vessels sailing in British waters would be seized.

Black Sea fleet frigate Admiral Grigorovich is said to have accompanied a pair of shadow fleet ships on Wednesday, which were followed by a British naval vessel.

According to the newspaper, the vessel observed the flotilla off England’s south coast while RFA Tideforce, a Royal Fleet Auxiliary tanker, was in their wake.

It comes after the prime minister last month said that the Navy will intercept Russia’s shadow fleet. The armed forces and British law enforcement are now able to board and halt sanctioned vessels that are passing through UK waters.

Sir Keir’s announcement came in conjunction with European allies in an attempt to cut off funding for Moscow’s war with Ukraine,

It is understood that Russia's shadow fleet consists of approximately 700 vessels, carrying around 40 per cent of all Russian oil exports. The UK has sanctioned 544 Russian shadow fleet vessels to date.

They illicitly ship oil and other goods out of Russia by flying the flags of other countries, with the aim of evading sanctions imposed by the West since the invasion of Ukraine began.

Sir Keir gave approval for British forces to begin seizing Russian shadow fleet tankers on 26 March.

Closing off British waters to the shadow fleet is aimed at forcing the Russian vessels into taking longer, more costly sea routes, or risk being intercepted by the UK.

Sir Keir said: “We are living in an increasingly volatile and dangerous world, facing threats from different fronts across the world every day.

“As prime minister, my first duty is to keep this country safe and protect British interests here and abroad.

“Putin is rubbing his hands at the war in the Middle East because he thinks higher oil prices will let him line his pockets.

“That’s why we’re going after his shadow fleet even harder, not just keeping Britain safe but starving Putin’s war machine of the dirty profits that fund his barbaric campaign in Ukraine.

“He and his cronies should be in no doubt, we will always defend our sovereignty and stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.”

British forces have already been involved in tracking shadow fleet vessels for several years, and have supported operations by other countries to seize the ships.

In January, the UK assisted in the seizure of the oil tanker Marinera by the US.

Renowned wildlife cameraman Doug Allan, who worked on iconic BBC series including Planet Earth, Frozen Planet and The Blue Planet, has died at the age of 74 while trekking in Nepal.

Often collaborating closely with Sir David Attenborough, Allan was widely celebrated as a “true pioneer” of wildlife filmmaking.

He won multiple Bafta and Emmy awards, and in 2024 he was appointed an OBE for his significant contributions to broadcast media and environmental awareness.

His management company, Jo Sarsby Management, confirmed his death, noting he died “immersed in nature and surrounded by friends”.

“A true pioneer of wildlife film-making, Doug captured some of the most breathtaking and intimate moments in the natural world,” the statement said.

“Doug leaves behind a visual legacy that few could ever match. His work brought audiences closer to the wonders of our planet, inspiring awe, understanding and deep respect for the planet."

open image in gallery Doug Allan died ‘immersed in nature and surrounded by friends’ ( Doug Allan )

The statement concluded by remembering his “unforgettable kindness and his extraordinary talent”, adding: “It has been an honour and a privilege to represent Doug as his agent and to know him as a friend for over 30 years. He was a true gentleman and he will be profoundly missed.

“Our thoughts are with his family, friends, colleagues across the wildlife film-making industry and the many people around the world who admired his work.”

Originally from Dunfermline in Fife, Allan’s connection with the natural world began with a marine biology degree from Stirling University in 1973.

His interest in filming wildlife blossomed during his tenure as a research diver at the British Antarctic Survey station on the Antarctic Signy Island in 1976.

He once recounted how a serendipitous encounter with Sir David Attenborough ultimately set him on his path to becoming a celebrated wildlife cameraman.

open image in gallery David Attenborough was the catalyst for Allan’s career as a wildlife filmmaker ( BBC )

“When I graduated (from Stirling University) I came out and did various jobs to do with diving, went to the Red Sea to work with some biologists, worked for a year with Bill Abernethy, who was Scotland’s last full-time professional pearl fisherman,” Allan explained in a previous interview.

“Then I went to the Antarctic and that’s when I as a diver discovered photography.”

Describing the moment he decided to pursue wildlife filmmaking, he recalled: “It was a chance meeting with David Attenborough, of all people, in 1981. He turned up in our base with a small film crew.

“I helped him for a couple of days and quite literally at the end of those two days I looked at the cameraman and thought, ‘You know, you are doing all the things I like doing’.”

He added: “The next trip to the Antarctic I bought a 16mm movie camera and in the wonderful naiveness of youth I went and did some filming of emperor penguins and sold the footage to BBC when I went back. That’s where it all started.”

News.content:

From April until August I can’t open the windows. I make my boyfriend shower before he gets in bed, smear Vaseline around my nostrils, eat local honey, and spend too much money on Allevia (fexofenadine), lubricating eye drops, super strength nasal sprays and prescription inhalers. Still, I can barely breathe, because the pollen has come – and if it were down to natural selection, I wouldn’t make it out of the ever-lengthening hay fever season alive.

This might all sound incredibly dramatic. But, as anyone who suffers from extreme allergies will know, it really is that debilitating. The morning after a high pollen count day, I often struggle to get out of bed as I battle through a so-called “hay fever hangover”, which depletes my energy, increases brain fog and, consequently, exacerbates my depression.

When social invitations come in, I second guess them. A picnic? In this state? Better to just stay home.

Hay fever has been getting steadily worse in the UK in recent years; 2025 was nothing short of a snot-filled apocalypse with a “pollen bomb” hitting London as early as April. This year, we’ve been granted even less mercy, with sneezing and scratchy throats starting thanks to “very high” tree pollen levels in (what should be) the winter month of February.

As such, allergists have warned that we’re in for a “bumper pollen season” ahead of us, recommending hay fever sufferers “start getting those antihistamine tablets from the pharmacy” stat. But I’m afraid (both in the apologetic and fearful sense of the term), that is simply not going to cut it. I need stronger drugs, a hazmat suit, or a banned third option.

open image in gallery Symptoms started in as early as February this year due to very high tree pollen levels ( Getty/iStock )

Hay fever jabs were available on the NHS until 2018, when the health service discontinued them due to safety concerns and a lack of evidence supporting their long-term effectiveness.

Potential side effects of this Kenalog (triamcinolone acetonide) injection can include abdominal pain, loss of bone density, depression, blindness and even death. Yet still, the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) found that 45 per cent of pharmacies surveyed had received queries from patients about the jab to relieve allergy symptoms last spring.

“The NHS evaluated everything and decided that it wasn’t suitable,” says Dr Leyla Hannbeck, CEO of the Independent Pharmacies Association. “It can weaken your immune system and that opens you up to infections which can have a long term impact on people,” she explains. “It’s not licensed in the UK as a treatment for hay fever anymore. So, if clinics are offering it to people as an allergy therapy – they shouldn’t be.”

With a quick Google, you can find private health clinics (and even beauty salons) offering the steroid injection for between £75 and £90 – and, despite the troubling health risks, there are sufferers desperate enough to chance the precarious cure. “My life has been changed already,” my friend Nancy tells me two days after her annual Kenalog jab. “Within 48 hours there’s already a noticeable difference,” she says.

open image in gallery In demand: 45 per cent of pharmacies have had queries about hay fever jabs ( Getty/iStock )

One of the many ways recipients of the Kenalog jab dismiss their concerns about the injection’s side effects is by pointing out that the steroid is safely used to treat other medical conditions, such as arthritis. “But remember, in that instance it will go into a joint. So, it’s going to stay in that joint,” points out allergist professor Adam Fox. “Whereas, with hay fever, you’re injecting it into your bum, which gets a wider circulation. The worry is it could have a potential impact on bone health, which increases the risk of fractures when you’re older.”

He concedes: “It would be disingenuous to suggest that it doesn’t work. There are a lot of people whose lives were absolutely blighted by horrendous hay fever and this was the only thing that did the job…but there are people that are going to be at particular risk.

“The worry is about bone health, so if you’re overweight, have a history of osteoporosis, or are a smoker, all of those things with an enormous whack of steroids is a bad combination,” Fox warns.

So, are our only options to suffer or take supreme risk? Well, actually, no. Despite me going to GP appointments every year, asking for help, and receiving none, Dr Fox tells me there is another alternative here: allergen immunotherapy (AIT) aka pollen desensitisation. The problem is, barely anybody knows about it – including those with medical degrees.

“Unfortunately, awareness amongst doctors in the UK is not good,” says Fox. “One of the main issues is that there’s very little taught about allergy on the medical school curriculum, so awareness is really poor. The likelihood that your doctor will even know that there’s something that goes above and beyond nasal sprays and antihistamines is low. They don’t even realise there’s something they could refer you for.”

Immunotherapy works by giving people a regular dose of the pollen allergen – either in an injection or pill – in order to reset their immune response over the course of three years. Desensitisation is highly effective, with NHS clinical trials showing the average improvement as 30 per cent in year one, 50 per cent in year two and 70 per cent in year three; But you have to start early. “If you wanted to be desensitised to tree pollen, where the season typically starts in around February, you should be starting treatment around October time,” explains Fox. “Whereas, if it’s for grass pollen, you need to start by the end of January.”

The treatment isn’t a total cure (you may still have to take antihistamines) but it does provide enough relief to live a normal life. “A good result would be that you’d change into somebody who, if they take their regular medication, can feel ok,” says Fox. “It doesn’t mean you’re going to throw away your antihistamines forever. Some people report feeling completely better, most people just noticed a marked improvement.”

open image in gallery Sufferers are mainly directed towards over the counter tablets and nasal sprays ( Getty/iStock )

Frankly, after decades of hay fever hell, I feel more than a little pissed to discover this option was invented in 1911. Yet, only last year, the National Institute of Clinical and Healthcare Excellence – who make recommendations to the NHS about whether treatments are worthwhile – found that it would be economically beneficial for the healthcare service to more widely prescribe immunotherapy to the right patients.

So far, the body has recommended a tree pollen tablet called Itulazax to the NHS – and are looking into grass pollen next. “We hope that because of that recommendation access to these treatments gets better,” says Fox. “But in reality, there are still very significant barriers.”

Aside from lack of GP knowledge, there are very few specialist allergy clinics that people can be referred to in the UK. “You’ll be in a queue behind people who’ve had anaphylaxis to nuts and all the other allergic issues,” says Fox. “We’re very limited compared to other countries and, as a consequence, waiting times are predictably long.

“If you look across Europe, for every person who gets desensitised to pollen in the UK, hundreds of people are desensitised in Germany. There’s just no comparison between other developed healthcare economies and the UK. We are really lagging in this particular area.”

open image in gallery ‘Really lagging’: Allergist Adam Fox is campaigning for better allergy services in the UK ( ITV )

If you take the leap and seek the treatment privately, costs are, unsurprisingly, high. For the same sublingual immunotherapy tablet that has the approval on the NHS, Fox says you’re looking at around £130 a month, which equates to around £4,200 for the full three years.

On Monday, 20 April, British allergy experts will come together to publish the first National Allergy Strategy, outlining to the government what the UK can do better in allergy services. “The key central point is that there are great treatments available, but people just aren’t getting access to them,” says Fox. “So, patients don’t know about them.”

Next hay fever season, I’ll be sure to ask my GP about (or possibly even educate them on) allergen immunotherapy. But, sadly, it’s too late for that for this year’s imminent pollen bomb that’s set to impact one in four of us in the UK in the coming, sneeze-inducing, weeks.

As I look down the barrel of another spring time spent exhausted and unable to breathe, I decide that the risks, for me, are worth it and book in for the Kenalog injection. Within 48 hours, I feel a miraculous difference. Yet still, anxiety lingers over going against the NHS’s advice. Hopefully soon, I won’t have to gamble my health to get the help I need.

For the fifth time in his boxing career, Tyson Fury is set to come out of retirement, and he will do so against Arslanbek Makhmudov this weekend.

Fury, a former two-time heavyweight champion, will box Makhmudov in the Briton’s first fight since December 2024, when he was outpointed by Oleksandr Usyk for the second time in eight months.

Fury, 37, is still desperate for a trilogy bout with Usyk, who holds the unified belts, after the Ukrainian handed the “Gypsy King” (34-2-1, 24 KOs) the first losses of his professional career.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury (left) and upcoming opponent Arslanbek Makhmudov ( Getty )

Whether or not that match-up awaits in Fury’s future, he will first have to overcome Russia’s Makhmudov (21-2, 19 KOs). The pair will clash in a main-event bout in London, with Conor Benn in action in the co-main event.

Against Regis Prograis, Benn will enter the ring for the first time since he surprisingly defected from his longtime promoter Eddie Hearn, and for the first time since avenging the sole loss of his pro career. The British welterweight was beaten by Chris Eubank Jr last April, but Benn dropped and outpointed his bitter rival in a November rematch.

Here’s all you need to know:

When is the fight?

Fury vs Makhmudov will take place on Saturday 11 April, at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. Exact timings have not yet been confirmed, but the main card is expected to begin at 7pm BST (11am PT / 1pm CT / 2pm ET), with main-event ring walks from 10pm BST (2pm PT / 4pm CT / 5pm ET).

How can I watch it?

The event will stream live exclusively on Netflix worldwide. It will be available to all existing subscribers; in other words, the event will not be a pay-per-view.

Fury – 2/9; Makhmudov – 7/2; draw – 16/1

Benn – 1/9; Prograis – 5/1; draw – 20/1

Rory McIlroy is among the early starters on the opening day of The Masters as the defending champion returns a year on from his stunning victory at Augusta.

McIlroy sensationally ended his long quest to win a Green Jacket when he completed the career Grand Slam a year ago, with the Northern Irishman now bidding to make more history by joining a select group of players to win back-to-back Masters.

The 36-year-old is now free from the burden and pressure of ending his major drought and will now be targeting more success, but a stacked field stands in his way - including world No 1 and 2024 Masters champion Scottie Scheffler and rival Bryson DeChambeau.

There is also a healthy group of contenders who will hope to keep the Green Jacket in European hands, with Jon Rahm, Tommy Fleetwood, Matt Fitzpatrick, Robert MacIntyre and last year’s runner-up Justin Rose all hoping to make a charge.

News.content:
